title: Mirabai
hook: a song signs its own name in the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and the song travels on

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai at a closed door in Vrindavan, answering that there was only one man there. Did a door close on you, and how did you answer? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.

This week, three women's voices. Shakuntala, told twice, in an epic and in a play. Andal refusing a mortal groom, questioning a conch, and dreaming her wedding. And Mira, dancing in bells and talking her way through a closed door. Here's something they share. What reaches us of each one has been carried, retold, sung, by people who loved them. Mira's songs show it plainly, because they end with a signature. Today, to close the week, the last line of a Mira song.
screen: `THREE WOMEN'S VOICES THIS WEEK.` → `CARRIED BY PEOPLE WHO LOVED THEM.` → `THE LAST LINE OF A SONG.`

segments.voice: Listen to how a Mira song ends. Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar. Mira's Lord is Giridhar, the clever one who lifted the mountain. The phrase comes back at the close of song after song sung in her name, like a seal pressed into wax. Singers call that kind of closing name a chhap, a stamp. It tells you whose song it is. Now ask how these songs reach us. By being sung: wandering singers, temple gatherings, women singing at home, families passing down the words they knew. And as they're sung, the same song can turn up in different words in different places. So when a song ends with Mira's stamp, what it promises is a voice and a lineage, not a notarized author. That raises an honest question, and the songs can't settle it: which lines go back to Mira's own lips? Some readers sort the songs into older and newer. Others say the question misses the point, since a song stays alive by being sung, and changing a little in every mouth. Both views take her seriously. Last, the stamp does something gentle. Whoever sings the song, wherever, ends by stepping aside: not my Lord, but Mira's Lord. Each singer lends Mira their voice for a few minutes, and Mira lends them her love. That's how a woman who, tradition says, left a palace with almost nothing is still being sung.
screen: `MIRA'S LORD IS GIRIDHAR` · `THE CHHAP, A STAMP` · `CARRIED FROM MOUTH TO MOUTH` · `EACH SINGER LENDS MIRA A VOICE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: looking back over the week. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring back the three women, one at a time. Shakuntala, standing her ground. Andal, with her conch and her dream. Mira, with bells on her feet. Let each one stay for a few breaths. Notice which voice stays with you longest, without deciding why. Then let them all go, and rest in the breath. If you pray, you can give thanks for whoever carried their stories to you. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai. Her songs end with a stamp, Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and they've traveled from mouth to mouth, changing as they go. Today's word.
Your line: Mirabai. Today, pass something on that someone gave you: a recipe, a saying, a song, with their name attached. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.
